av_event.line_text: So is that all week then, the pharmacy?
av_event.what: A tall teenage boy in a hoodie walks through the kitchen behind Tracey. He opens the fridge, takes out a carton and leaves the frame. Tracey doesn't turn round.

text:
A: Hiya! Oh, there you are. Can you hear me alright?
B: Hi, yes, I can hear you. Hi.
A: Lovely. I'm Tracey. Did you do that puzzle thing at the start? I was useless at it, honestly, I just sat there going round in circles.
B: Erm, I'm Maricel. Yeah, I did it. I think I got stuck on the last one as well, so.
A: Oh thank God, it's not just me then. I thought, they're gonna think I'm thick. So what do you do, Maricel? Sorry, am I saying that right?
B: Yes, Maricel, that's right. Erm, I'm a pharmacy technician. In Leyton, a little independent pharmacy.
A: Oh right, so like the one behind the counter doing the prescriptions?
B: Sort of, yeah. I do the checking, so when the dispensing's done I check it's the right drug, right strength, right patient. And I do a lot for care homes, sorting out their medicines when people come out of hospital. It's quite fiddly but I like it, honestly. You have to be very careful.
A: Ar, I bet. I couldn't do that, I'd be terrified of getting it wrong. I'm a fitness instructor, at the leisure centre in Walsall. Aqua aerobics, circuits, and I do a seated class for the older ones.
B: Oh, seated exercise. That's nice. A lot of my care home patients would probably benefit from that, to be fair.
A: They love it. I've got one lady, she's ninety-one, comes every Tuesday on the bus, never misses. Mind you, half of 'em come for the chat and the cup of tea after, not the exercise. Sorry, am I going on?
B: No, no. That's lovely. I think that's important, the chat part. With the elderly patients, a lot of the time they just want someone to listen.
A: That's it exactly.
B: Mm.
A: So is that all week then, the pharmacy?
B: Three and a half days. I keep the rest for pottery, mostly. I do a wheel class every week.
A: Oh, is that them mugs behind you in your photo? On the shelf? I noticed them when we was doing the pictures bit.
B: Yes! Erm, yeah, those are mine. The blue speckled ones. I sell a few on Instagram, just small.
A: Get away, you made them? They look like proper shop ones. I thought you'd bought them somewhere posh.
B: Thank you. Honestly, the glaze is the hard part. You do a test tile and it comes out one colour, then the actual mug comes out completely different. The last batch was supposed to be green and it came out sort of brown. Like tea.
A: Ha, well, I'd still drink out of it. I'm not arty at all, me. I'd make an ashtray by accident.
B: Everyone says that, but it's mostly practice. You'd probably be good, you know, with the coordination and everything.
A: Maybe. I don't get the time though, really. I've got my lad, Kieran, he's sixteen, so I'm forever driving him to football and feeding him. He eats me out of house and home.
B: Sixteen. I can imagine.
A: Two loaves a week, I'm not joking. And my mum's ten minutes up the road, so I'm back and forth there as well. Is your family near you?
B: Erm, no. My mum's in Manila, in the Philippines. And my brother. I go every other year, for a month usually.
A: Oh bless you, that's a long way. Do you miss her?
B: Yeah. Yeah, I do. It's hard, she's getting older. You feel a bit guilty, you know, being here.
A: I know what you mean. My mum's knee's playing up and I worry, and I'm only round the corner, so I can't imagine being all that way.
B: Mm. It's okay. We video call a lot, like this.
A: Well, that's something. And when you go over, do you just stay with her the whole month, or do you get to—
